title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E555 §§29 (end of the Scholion), pp. 182–183 of Opuscula analytica I. Euler first proves the 'Theorem 3' of §28 and then derives a log-integral theorem from the 'more abstruse' theorem of §23.

(1) Notation and proof of §28. Euler takes his notation from his older memoir on such integrals: (p/q) = ∫_0^1 y^{p-1}(1-y^n)^{q/n-1} dy. In modern terms this is (1/n)B(p/n, q/n).
- The claim to be proved is (λ/λ)(λ/(n-λ)) = [2π cos(λπ/n)/(n sin(λπ/n))]·(λ/(n-2λ)).
- He uses the reflection formula: if q+r=n, then (q/r) = π/(n sin(qπ/n)), i.e. B(a,1-a) = π/sin πa. This gives (λ/(n-λ)) = π/(n sin(λπ/n)).
- What remains is (λ/λ) = 2cos(λπ/n)·(λ/(n-2λ)).
- For this he uses his symmetric three-term relation: if p+q+r=n, then (p/q)/sin(rπ/n) = (p/r)/sin(qπ/n) = (q/r)/sin(pπ/n). In modern form this says Γ(a)Γ(b)Γ(c)/π is symmetric when a+b+c=1.
- Taking p=q=λ, r=n-2λ and using sin(2θ)=2 sinθ cosθ finishes the proof.
- With m=λ/n the result reads B(m,m) = 2cos(mπ)·B(m,1-2m), equivalently B(m,m)B(m,1-m) = 2π cot(mπ)·B(m,1-2m).

(2) The §23 theorem and its consequence. Euler quotes the §23 result (with n playing the role of an exponent m):
  π/sin(mπ)·∫x^m(1-x)^{m-1}dx = π/(2 sin mπ)·B(m,m) = ∫(dx/x)·∫_0^x t^{m-1}(1-t)^{-m}dt.
- He substitutes x=y^n, m=λ/n.
- He replaces B(m,m) by 2cos(mπ)B(m,1-2m), using step (1).
- He integrates the iterated integral by parts: ∫_0^1 F(x)dx/x = -∫ x^{m-1}(1-x)^{-m} ln x dx.
- The result is the claimed 'noteworthy theorem': -∫_0^1 y^{λ-1}(1-y^n)^{-λ/n} ln y dy = [π/(n tan(λπ/n))]·∫_0^1 y^{λ-1}(1-y^n)^{-2λ/n} dy.
- For λ=1 this becomes the proportion π/n : tan(π/n) = ∫ ln(1/y)(1-y^n)^{-1/n}dy : ∫(1-y^n)^{-2/n}dy.
- In modern terms the claim is -ψ(m)-γ = B(m,m)/2, equivalently -ψ(m)-γ = cos(mπ)Γ(m)Γ(1-2m)/Γ(1-m).

Overall purpose: these are corollaries showing what the interpolation-series method of the memoir yields for Beta-type integrals.
errors: Part (1) is correct. The reflection formula, the three-term sine relation and the identity B(m,m) = 2cos(mπ)B(m,1-2m) all check out with Gamma functions.

The §23 'abstruse theorem' as quoted here is false: π/(2 sin mπ)·B(m,m) = ∫(dx/x)∫_0^x t^{m-1}(1-t)^{-m}dt.
- The right side equals -∫x^{m-1}(1-x)^{-m}ln x dx = (π/sin mπ)(-ψ(m)-γ). The identity would therefore require -ψ(m)-γ = B(m,m)/2.
- The two sides agree only in the leading term 1/m as m→0.
- Counterexample m=1/2: the true value ∫_0^1 ln x/√(x(1-x))dx = -2π ln 2 gives 2π ln 2 ≈ 4.355, whereas the theorem gives π²/2 ≈ 4.935.

Consequently the final 'Theorema non minus notatu dignum' and the λ=1 proportion are also false.
- Check n=4, λ=1: ∫_0^1 ln(1/y)(1-y^4)^{-1/4}dy = (π√2/16)(π/2+3 ln 2) ≈ 1.0136. A direct series sum Σ c_k/(4k+1)² also gives ≈1.013.
- But (π/4)·tan(π/4)·∫_0^1 dy/√(1-y^4) ≈ 0.7854 × 1.31103 ≈ 1.0297.
- The proportion therefore fails by about 1.6%.

Since the reduction steps on this page are valid, the error must originate in §23, presumably from mis-summing an interpolation series. Alternatively, the theorem may have been mis-copied when restated here. Which of the two cannot be checked from this page alone.

ideas.what: Notation (p/q) for ∫y^{p-1}(1-y^n)^{q/n-1}dy and the reflection value (q/r) = π/(n sin(qπ/n)) when q+r=n
ideas.modern_name: Beta function B(a,1-a) = π/sin πa (Euler reflection formula)
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier memoirs on integrals ∫x^{p-1}(1-x^n)^{q/n-1}dx (Observationes circa integralia formularum..., around E321), Institutiones calculi integralis

ideas.modern_name: Γ(a)Γ(b)Γ(c)/π symmetric when a+b+c=1 (consequence of the reflection formula)
ideas.where_published: Same earlier memoir on the (p/q) integrals, which Euler cites as 'olim commentatus'

ideas.modern_name: Beta/Gamma identity following from reflection plus the sine duplication formula
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (special case of his Beta relations)
ideas.where_published: E555 §28–29 (this memoir); closely related relations appear in his earlier integral memoirs

ideas.what: Converting an iterated integral ∫dx/x ∫... into -∫(...)ln x dx by integration by parts
ideas.modern_name: Integration by parts; log-moment of the Beta integrand (∂B/∂a = B(ψ(a)-ψ(a+b)))
ideas.where_published: Common in Euler's integral calculus work

ideas.what: Claimed closed form -∫y^{λ-1}(1-y^n)^{-λ/n}ln y dy = π/(n tan(λπ/n))∫y^{λ-1}(1-y^n)^{-2λ/n}dy
ideas.modern_name: Would amount to -ψ(m)-γ = B(m,m)/2, which is false

missed.claim: The 'more abstruse' theorem of §23 and the derived log-integral theorem and proportion are false. In modern terms they assert ψ(m)+γ = -B(m,m)/2, which fails already at m=1/2 (2 ln 2 vs π/2). Unless the Opera omnia editor flagged it, this is an uncorrected error in a published Euler memoir.
missed.quote: Multo magis autem abstrusum est Theorema supra (23) erutum ... hincque porro istud Theorema non minus notatu dignum ... π/n : tang. π/n = ∫dy l(1/y)/ⁿ√(1-y^n) : ∫dy/ⁿ√(1-y^n)²
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It shows a failure mode of Euler's interpolation method: an identity that is correct only to leading order as m→0 was presented as exact. This is relevant for historians assessing the reliability of the interpolation-series method, and for anyone citing E555's integral formulas.

deep.surprise_reason: The proof of §28 is routine Beta/Gamma manipulation from Euler's earlier memoirs. The notable point is that the 'abstruse' theorem and its corollary are demonstrably false. A modest surprise; the Opera omnia editors may already have noted it (unsure).
transcription_corrections: Page numbers are 182 and 183 (headers '-) 182 (-' and '-) 183 (-'), not 162/163.

First displayed formula of p.183: π/(sin. nπ)∫x^n dx(1-x)^{n-1} = ∫(dx/x)∫x^{n-1}dx/(1-x)^n. The second form has π/(2 sin. nπ)∫x^{n-1}dx(1-x)^{n-1}; this is consistent with B(n+1,n) = B(n,n)/2, so the '[?]' marks can be removed.
In the final proportion the left integrand is dy·l(1/y)/ⁿ√(1-y^n) and the right is dy/ⁿ√(1-y^n)².
